newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea slams South for breakdown of food talks.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea slams South for breakdown of food talks.

text.p: North Korea on Tuesday slammed rival South Korea for the breakdown of talks on food aid between the countries' Red Cross organisations, calling Seoul's attitude "eccentric and incomprehensible".
Negotiations on speeding up food aid to the famine-stricken North began last Friday and broke down on Monday. They were the first such inter-Korean Red Cross talks in almost five years.

"No agreement was reached at the contact (meeting) due to the South side's eccentric and incomprehensible attitude," the North's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said in a report monitored in Tokyo.

"It is empty talk and a sheer waste of time to discuss the procedures and method of the offering, with the South side's position remaining unclear," KCNA quoted a spokesman for the North Korean Red Cross as saying.
"When South Korea was hit by floods in the past, we made clear the names and quantity of relief goods...and supplied all of them in days without any condition," the spokesman said.
"If the South Korean Red Cross truly wants to do something with compatriotic and humanitarian feelings, it should follow the good example shown by the North in the past," he said.
The talks are stalled over how much and how South Korean grain would be delivered.
The South Korean Red Cross insisted on opening more channels for direct shipments of grain while the North wanted a pledge of an exact aid amount before it would agree to anything.
However, North Korea left open the possibility of future negotiations on condition that the South agreed to the North's demands.
"We will meet with the South side anytime when it notifies us of the date of the contact after preparing the relief goods in a responsible manner," the North Korean spokesman said.

South Korean Red Cross representatives also said on Monday that the talks would resume in the near future by way of a direct telephone link in the town of Panmunjom that straddles the border between the two Koreas.
The two Koreas have remained technically at war because their 1950-53 conflict ended only in a truce.

North Korea has slid into famine after being hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996. Officials have reported deaths of children from malnutrition and farmers eating sawdust to fill out their diet.

The U.N. World Food Programme estimates that North Korea has only enough food to last it until June and that after that its 24 million people will have to wait for the next harvest in October and November.

South Korea, the United States and Japan are scheduled to hold talks in Tokyo on Wednesday to discuss food shortages in North Korea and ways to encourage Pyongyang to join peace talks aimed at hammering out a permanent treaty to end the Korean War.
Pyongyang last month agreed to join the talks if it was first guaranteed large-scale food aid, U.S. diplomatic recognition and an easing of trade sanctions.
